skills.title: Name the main social science disciplines (geography, history, political science, economics) and the core question each one asks
Classify a question or issue by the discipline(s) that study it
Analyse one real issue through several disciplinary lenses and show how they connect
Explain how social scientists use evidence and listen to multiple perspectives

expectations: Social science studies people and society: how we live together, use space and resources, govern ourselves and change over time.

Geography asks where and why there (people, places, environment); history asks what changed over time and how we know (sources); political science asks who decides and how power and rules work; economics asks how people make choices about scarce resources (production, distribution, consumption).
Real issues (a flood, a price rise, an election) need several disciplines at once because causes and effects cross subject boundaries.
Social scientists work from evidence (maps, data, documents, inscriptions, interviews), check sources, and compare different viewpoints before concluding.

skills.title: Describe the Earth's layers (crust, mantle, core) and the idea of moving tectonic plates
Explain internal (endogenic) processes: plate movement, folding, faulting, earthquakes and volcanoes
Distinguish external (exogenic) processes: weathering, erosion, transport and deposition
Identify landforms made by rivers, wind, glaciers and sea waves and name their agent
Reason cause-and-effect from Earth processes to hazards and human life

expectations: The Earth has a thin rocky crust, a hot mantle and a metallic core; the crust and upper mantle are broken into large plates that move slowly over the mantle.

Internal forces build landforms: when plates push together, rock layers fold into mountains (the Himalayas formed as the Indian plate pushed into the Eurasian plate and are still rising), while cracks and breaks (faults) and sudden slips cause earthquakes; magma reaching the surface forms volcanoes.

External forces wear landforms down: weathering breaks rock in place (heat-cold, water, plant roots, chemicals); erosion is removal and transport of that material by running water, wind, ice and waves; deposition drops it elsewhere.

Each agent leaves typical landforms: rivers make V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains and deltas; wind makes sand dunes and mushroom rocks; glaciers make U-shaped valleys and moraines; waves make sea cliffs, arches, stacks and beaches.
The surface is always changing — slowly (millimetres a year) or suddenly (earthquakes, landslides) — and this shapes where people farm, build and face hazards.

skills.title: Describe the composition of the atmosphere (main gases and their rough shares)
Name the layers of the atmosphere in order and one key feature of each
Distinguish weather from climate
Explain the factors that control climate (latitude, altitude, distance from sea, winds, ocean currents, relief)

expectations: The atmosphere is a blanket of gases held by gravity: about 78% nitrogen, about 21% oxygen, small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) and variable water vapour and dust.

Layers from the ground up: troposphere (where weather happens; temperature falls with height), stratosphere (contains the ozone layer that absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays; calm, used by jets), mesosphere (meteors burn up; coldest), thermosphere (very thin air, ionosphere reflects radio waves, auroras), then the exosphere.
Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place for a short time (hours or days); climate is the average pattern over a long period (about 30 years or more).

Climate is controlled by latitude (angle of the sun's rays), altitude (air gets colder with height, about 6.5 °C per km in the troposphere), distance from the sea (sea moderates temperature), winds and pressure belts, ocean currents, and relief (mountains block winds and cause rain on one side).
Using these factors we can explain differences, e.g. Bengaluru (about 900 m high on a plateau) is cooler than Chennai (near sea level) even though they are at similar latitudes.

For most of human history people were hunter-gatherers using stone tools: large hand axes in the Palaeolithic, tiny microliths in the Mesolithic, and polished stone tools in the Neolithic; they used fire and made rock paintings such as those at Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh).

About 10,000 years ago people in several regions began farming and domesticating animals (in the subcontinent, Mehrgarh is an early farming site); settled life produced food surpluses, so some people could become craftspeople, traders or leaders.

expectations: Many states, not one, shaped India up to 1000 CE: janapadas and the sixteen mahajanapadas (around the 6th century BCE), the Mauryan empire (about 321–185 BCE), later kingdoms such as the Satavahanas, Kushanas, Guptas (from about 320 CE), Harsha, and southern powers such as the Pallavas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and Cholas.

Political forms varied: kingdoms ruled by rajas, and ganas or sanghas like the Vajji confederacy where groups of leaders decided in assemblies; later inscriptions such as those at Uttaramerur (Chola period, 10th century CE) describe village assemblies choosing committees.

States collected taxes from farmers, traders and artisans, kept armies and officials, and gave land grants to temples, Brahmins and officials; rulers like Ashoka issued edicts about dhamma and good conduct.
Society and economy rested on farming, with crafts, guilds (shrenis) of merchants and artisans, coins, towns and long-distance trade by land and sea.

skills.title: State the meaning of democracy as rule by the people and its key features

expectations: Democracy is a form of government in which the rulers are chosen by the people and are answerable to them.

Key features: final decision-making power rests with elected representatives; elections are free, fair and regular with a real choice; one person, one vote, one value; the government works within the limits of a constitution and the rule of law; citizens' rights (speech, association, equality) are protected.

Democracy is more than voting: it includes discussion, accountability between elections, independent institutions (courts, election commission, free media) and respect for minority rights, not just majority rule.

Arguments for: it is more accountable, improves decisions through discussion, enhances dignity and equality, allows peaceful correction of mistakes and handles differences; arguments against: decisions can be slow, leaders may change often, and money or popularity can distort it — but these weaknesses can be addressed within democracy.
Ideas of collective decision-making have long roots, including assemblies in ancient Indian ganas and village sabhas, and modern India's democracy is built on its Constitution.

skills.title: Explain why representative democracies need elections

expectations: In a large democracy people cannot all decide every matter directly, so they choose representatives through regular elections that let them pick, judge and replace their leaders.

India is divided into constituencies (543 for the Lok Sabha); some are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes; every citizen aged 18 or above can be on the voters' list (electoral roll) and vote — universal adult franchise.

Steps: announcement of the schedule, nominations with sworn details of the candidate's criminal record, assets and education, scrutiny, campaign, polling by secret ballot using EVMs with VVPAT slips, and counting; NOTA lets a voter reject all candidates.

The Election Commission of India is an independent constitutional body that conducts elections; once it announces the schedule, the model code of conduct applies, limiting what parties and governments may do (for example, no new schemes announced to sway voters, no appeals on religious or caste lines).

Seats are won by first past the post: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority; the party or coalition with a majority of seats in the Lok Sabha forms the government.

skills.title: Explain scarcity: unlimited wants and limited resources

Identify the opportunity cost of a choice as the value of the next best alternative given up

expectations: Scarcity means our wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them (money, time, land, labour, materials) are limited, so everyone — rich or poor, person or country — must choose.

Needs are things essential for living (food, water, shelter, health); wants are things we desire beyond that; goods and services are produced using resources: land (natural resources), labour, capital (tools, machines, buildings) and entrepreneurship.
Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative given up — only the single best option forgone, not all of them, and not just the money price.
Societies must answer three basic questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom; households, businesses and governments all face trade-offs.
Even 'free' things have an opportunity cost, often time or resources that could have been used elsewhere.

skills.title: Explain how waves, tides and ocean currents form and how they differ

expectations: Waves are mostly caused by wind blowing over the surface; in a wave the water mainly moves up and down in circles, so the energy travels, not the water itself.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon (and the Sun); most coasts have two high and two low tides roughly every 24 hours 50 minutes; spring tides (largest) come at new and full moon, neap tides at the quarter moons.

Ocean currents are large, steady flows of water driven by winds, differences in temperature and salinity, and the Earth's rotation; warm currents warm nearby coasts and cold currents cool them; in the north Indian Ocean currents reverse with the monsoon.

Oceans give fish, salt, oil and gas (for example, Mumbai High), minerals, tidal and wave energy, and trade routes; India claims an Exclusive Economic Zone of 200 nautical miles; overfishing and pollution show that these resources must be used sustainably.

A tsunami is a series of very long waves caused mostly by undersea earthquakes (not by wind); after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, India set up an early warning centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad, which together with evacuation drills and cyclone shelters saves lives.

skills.title: Explain the biosphere, ecosystems and food chains as connected systems
Describe major biomes (rainforest, monsoon/deciduous forest, grassland, desert, tundra, taiga) by climate, plants and animals
Locate examples of biomes and biosphere reserves in India on a map and describe the core, buffer and transition zones
Evaluate conservation efforts, including community-led ones, weighing people's needs and nature's protection

expectations: The biosphere is the zone of the Earth where life exists, linking land, water and air; an ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and their non-living environment, with energy flowing through food chains.

A biome is a large region with a similar climate, vegetation and animal life: tropical rainforests (hot, wet all year, very rich biodiversity), tropical deciduous or monsoon forests (trees shed leaves in the dry season), grasslands, deserts (very little rain), taiga (coniferous forests) and tundra (very cold, short summer).

India has 18 biosphere reserves, such as the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (India's first, set up in 1986, across Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka) and the Sundarbans; many are part of UNESCO's world network.

A biosphere reserve has a protected core zone, a buffer zone for research and limited use, and a transition zone where people live and use resources sustainably — it protects nature together with people, not by removing them.

Conservation includes government programmes (such as Project Tiger, 1973) and community action (such as the Chipko movement and the Bishnoi community's protection of trees and blackbuck); good conservation balances livelihoods with protection.

Cause of rain: moist south-west monsoon winds hit the Ghats and rise, giving heavy rain; by the time winds reach western Rajasthan little moisture remains, and the Aravallis run parallel to the winds and do not force them up
Vegetation: heavy rain all through the season supports dense evergreen forests; scarce rain supports thorny shrubs and grasses
Animals: rainforests hold many species like lion-tailed macaques and hornbills; deserts hold animals adapted to dryness, like camels, desert foxes and great Indian bustards
Conclusion: biomes follow climate, especially rainfall and temperature, not borders

expectations: Between 1000 and 1700 CE many powers coexisted in the subcontinent: the Cholas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and Vijayanagara (from 1336) in the south; Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar; the Delhi Sultanate (from 1206) and later the Mughal empire (from 1526); the Ahoms in the north-east; and later the Marathas and Sikhs.

Regional powers resisted outside rule in different ways — battles, alliances and diplomacy, fortified capitals in hills and deserts, and sustained local administration — for example the Ahoms defeated a Mughal force at Saraighat (1671) and Shivaji founded a Maratha state, crowned at Raigad in 1674.

Societies also showed resilience by adapting: kingdoms built temples, forts, tanks and irrigation, supported trade and regional languages, and many rulers and communities exchanged ideas, styles and skills.

The Bhakti tradition (saints such as Basavanna, Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Sankardev and Tukaram) stressed personal devotion and often questioned empty ritual and social discrimination; Sufi saints taught devotion in a similar spirit; they composed in regional languages and reached ordinary people.
Historians use inscriptions, court chronicles, travellers' accounts, buildings and literature, and compare different perspectives, because court sources usually tell the story from the ruler's side.

expectations: India was connected to the wider world long before 1200 CE: Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, whose texts mention trade with a land called Meluhha, generally identified with the Indus region; Lothal in Gujarat had a dock-like structure.

Sailors used the seasonal monsoon winds to cross the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal; ports such as Muziris (Kerala) and Arikamedu (near Puducherry) traded pepper, spices, textiles and gems with the Roman world, as Roman coins and pottery found in south India show; overland routes linked India to Central Asia and China along the Silk Roads.

Ideas travelled with merchants, monks and scholars: Buddhism spread to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia; scholars like Xuanzang came to study at Nalanda; Indian numerals with zero passed through the Arab world to Europe.

In Southeast Asia, rulers adopted and adapted Sanskrit, Indian scripts, epics like the Ramayana (for example the Ramakien of Thailand) and temple architecture — Angkor Wat in Cambodia (12th century, first dedicated to Vishnu), Borobudur (Buddhist) and Prambanan (Hindu) in Java — blending them with local traditions.

Exchange was two-way: India received goods (gold, horses, silk, wine), ideas and people from other regions, and the spread of Indian culture happened mainly through trade, religion and choice rather than conquest.

skills.title: Distinguish power, authority and legitimacy
Explain ideas of authority in Indian political thought: danda, nyaya, rajadharma and matsya nyaya
Explain the limits on authority and the duties that come with it (welfare of subjects, rule of law)
Connect these ideas to democratic institutions today (Constitution, elected government, courts, accountability)

expectations: Power is the ability to make others act; authority is power that people accept as rightful (legitimate) — because it comes from law, tradition, consent or a fair process.

In Indian political thought, danda (literally the rod) stands for the state's power to enforce law and punish; texts such as Kautilya's Arthashastra argue that without danda there is matsya nyaya — the 'law of the fishes', where the big swallow the small.

Authority must be used with nyaya (justice) and according to rajadharma (the ruler's duty); the Arthashastra advises that punishment should be neither too harsh nor too mild but just, and that the ruler's good lies in the welfare of the people.

In a democracy, authority comes from the Constitution and the people: elected representatives make laws, the executive implements them, courts check that power is used lawfully, and everyone, including those in power, is under the rule of law.
Authority exists in many places — family, school, community, workplace — and in each case it is legitimate only when it is fair, accountable and used for the good of those it affects.

skills.title: Explain what entrepreneurship is and what entrepreneurs do (spot a problem, innovate, organise resources, take risk)

expectations: An entrepreneur spots a problem or need, comes up with an idea (product or service) to meet it, organises resources — land, labour, capital and materials — and takes the risk of success or failure.

A business plan states the problem, the customers, the product, costs, price, expected sales and how to fund it; money can come from savings, family, bank loans (e.g. MUDRA loans for small businesses), investors or grants.

Revenue is money earned from sales (price × quantity); cost is what is spent; profit = revenue − cost; a loss occurs when costs exceed revenue; fixed costs stay the same whatever the sales, variable costs rise with each unit made.

A startup is a new business built around an innovative idea and aiming to grow; India supports startups through Startup India (launched 2016), incubators at colleges, the Atal Innovation Mission and Atal Tinkering Labs in schools.

Entrepreneurship is not only for tech founders or the rich: small shops, cooperatives (such as Amul) and women-led enterprises (such as Lijjat Papad, started in 1959 by seven women in Mumbai) are enterprises too, and failure is a common step that entrepreneurs learn from.

skills.title: Prepare a simple budget: income, needs, wants and savings, and identify a surplus or deficit
Calculate simple interest and compound interest and compare them
Explain inflation and how it reduces the purchasing power of money
Compare saving and investment options by safety, return and liquidity, and practise safe banking

expectations: A budget plans how income will be used: list income, then expenses (needs first, then wants), and set aside savings first rather than saving only what is left; if income exceeds expenses there is a surplus, otherwise a deficit.

Simple interest is earned only on the original principal: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100; compound interest is earned on the principal plus past interest, so amount A = P × (1 + R/100)^T, and grows faster over time.

Inflation is a general rise in prices over time; it reduces what a fixed amount of money can buy, so savings must earn more than the inflation rate to grow in real terms (real return ≈ interest rate − inflation rate).

Options differ in safety, return and liquidity: savings accounts (safe, low return, easy to withdraw), fixed and recurring deposits, post office schemes and PPF (safe, fixed returns, locked for some time), and mutual funds or shares (higher possible return, higher risk); higher return usually comes with higher risk.
Safe banking: never share an OTP, PIN or password, check messages and links carefully, and know that bank deposits are insured by DICGC up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
